To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) we demonstrate that a simple randomization of simulator dynamics can enable a policy trained in a simulator to generalize to a physical robot; (2) we show that our approach is robust to large calibration errors and (3) we demonstrate that our approach enables the transfer of a policy trained with a single arm to a robot with multiple arms

we demonstrate a method that allows policies trained in simulation to transfer to the physical world without any training in the real world, and that the resulting policies can be robust to significant calibration errors.

randomizing the dynamics during training enables the policies to adapt to different dynamics, and this adaptivity enables the policy to generalize to the real world without additional training on the physical robot.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of simulating real robots in a way that allows the policies trained in simulation to transfer to the real world.
the problem of transferring control policies trained on simulators to their physical counterparts.
the problem of sim-to-real transfer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we are able to train a robotic arm in simulation, and then transfer the learned policy to a physical system, without any fine-tuning on the real world.
the proposed method is capable of transferring policies from simulation to the real world with high performance, and the policies are robust to calibration error.
our method allows the training of policies that can generalize to very different dynamics without any additional training on the physical robot.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we demonstrate how to use a simple simulator to develop policies that can be deployed on a real system without requiring any training data from it.

we have shown that it is possible to train policies that are robust to significant changes in the dynamics of a system, and that these policies can be deployed on the real world with minimal additional training.
we demonstrate how to use randomization to make policies more robust, which is an important step towards the development of safe and reliable robotic agents.
The main takeaway from our work is that
by training agents in environments that are significantly different from the real world, it is possible to develop policies that adapt to a variety of dynamics.
the key to bridging the reality gap is not to make simulators more realistic, but rather to make the policies robust to dynamics variations.

by randomizing the dynamics during the training process, we are able, in a principled manner, to develop policies that can adapt to a wide range of dynamics, including ones significantly different from those on which the policies have been trained.
